title: How companies buy AI video creation platforms now
summary: Security and AI councils now sign off before an AI video trial. What 2,055 buyer calls from 2024 to 2026 show about how companies buy AI video.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


- We analyzed 2,055 buyer calls from May 2024 to November 2026. Security came up on 8.6% of them in the first half of 2024 and on 31.9% from July to early November 2026.
- On discovery and demo calls, the most-asked single question was whether we're SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 certified (78 calls). "What does it cost?" came second, with 76.
- AI governance became its own approval step. An AI council that had to approve the tool came up on 26 calls, 22 of them in 2026. Buyers now ask where content is stored, which model providers see it, and whether the tool can be limited to approved ones.
- Budget approval is still the most-asked question of all 267 (113 calls), and it's a question about who signs off.
- Our thesis: AI video is now bought like infrastructure. For a growing share of companies, security and AI governance sign off before the trial starts, and the videos get judged second.


The way companies buy AI tools is changing. Across 1,020 discovery and demo calls since May 2024, the question buyers asked us most was whether Clueso is SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 certified. It came up on 78 calls, two more than “What does it cost?” Price still matters, but more buyers now come to a first call with their security team’s questions in hand.


Security was already climbing through 2025, and we think AI agents are what’s pushing it further. An agent can now record a walkthrough of your product and re-record it when the UI changes. That work used to take someone hours of recording and editing, and an agent does it for a fraction of the cost. In October 2026,[agents built 19% of the new videos made on Clueso](https://www.clueso.io/blog/ai-agent-video-study) .


An agent needs access to do that work accurately. It has to log in to your product to record it. To describe features correctly and follow the way your team works, it may also need your docs or your source code. Giving software that kind of access is new for most companies, and the people approving it are still working out three questions:


- How much access should an agent get?
- If someone misuses that access after it’s granted, who’s responsible?
- How do you make sure nothing the agent reads or touches leaks?


Our calls show those questions moving into the buying process. We went back through 2,055 recorded buyer calls from May 2024 to November 2026, pulled out every question a prospect or customer asked, and merged them into 267 distinct questions. In the first half of 2024, security came up on 13 of 152 buyer calls. From July to early November 2026, it came up on 221 of 692. Over the same stretch, pricing fell from 66.4% of calls to 58.2%.


Two years ago nobody asked us about agent access. Since November 2025, 38 calls have asked whether it’s safe to give an agent login credentials, and since July 2026, 36 have asked whether an agent needs access to the code repository.


Our thesis is that **AI video is now bought like infrastructure: once a tool can act inside your product, security and AI governance have to sign off before the trial starts, and the videos get judged second.** The answers to each security question are in[what enterprise buyers ask about AI video tools](https://www.clueso.io/blog/evaluating-enterprise-ai-video-tools) . This post is about the shift, what it means for whoever has to carry a tool through approval, and where our data runs out.

The line isn't smooth: security dipped in the first half of 2026 before reaching its highest share yet, and the earliest half-year rests on only 152 calls. Even so, a topic that came up on fewer than one call in ten now comes up on nearly one in three.


What surprised us more was where it comes up. Of the 96 calls where a buyer asked about SOC 2 or ISO 27001, 78 were discovery or demo calls. Only 35 calls in the entire set were dedicated security reviews, so buyers are bringing their security team's questions to the first conversation rather than saving them for a formal review.


Buyers have asked about certification early since 2024. The question that grew in 2026 was about the review process itself. "Our security review is required first: what do you need from us, and how long will it take?" came up on 91 calls, and 65 of them were in 2026. That's 71% of the question's calls in a year that holds 53% of all the buyer calls we analyzed. Requests for the actual documents, like the SOC 2 report and pen test results, came up on another 46.


For someone running customer education or product marketing, this changes who the first audience is. IT's questions now reach the first calls, sometimes before your team has seen a single video.


## AI councils now want to approve the tool before anyone tests it


Security reviews have been part of software buying for years. AI governance is newer, and in our calls it showed up at a different point in the purchase: before the trial.


"Our AI council has to approve any AI tool, even for a trial" first came up in May 2025. It has come up on 26 calls in all, 22 of them in 2026. Over the same period, buyers started asking which internal teams have to approve a vendor and in what order: IT, procurement, legal, the PMO, and an AI council. That question came up on 38 calls, starting in January 2025.


A third question shows the effect on the trial itself. "Can we test with our real content before the security review and contract?" came up on 20 calls. The first was in October 2025, and 19 were in 2026. These buyers wanted to evaluate the product properly, but their own policy didn't let them put company content into an unapproved AI tool. The trial waited for the review, or ran on generic content that didn't prove much.


None of this is unique to video. In the[IAPP's AI Governance Profession Report 2025](https://www.iapp.org/resources/article/ai-governance-profession-report) , published with Credo AI, 77% of the organizations surveyed in spring 2024 were already working on AI governance. What's specific to AI video is how much company material goes into it. A recording of an unreleased feature or an internal process walkthrough is exactly the kind of content a governance policy is written to protect.


The questions these committees ask are the ones you'd ask of a cloud provider. Do you train AI models on our content? That came up on 31 calls, 24 of them in 2026. Which third-party AI providers see it? Can our data stay in a specific region? Can we restrict the tool to models we've approved? That last question first came up in March 2026 and has come up on eight calls in all. Buyers ask these things of an AI video tool because it sends their content to model providers to do its job.


## Agents and MCP pushed AI video further into IT's territory


The newest questions in the data are about access, and they didn't exist two years ago. Once[AI agents](https://www.clueso.io/agents) could record and update videos by working inside a company's own product, buyers started asking what that agent would need to touch.


Whether it's safe to give an agent login credentials came up on 38 calls, all of them since November 2025. Whether an agent needs access to the source code repository came up on 36, all since July 2026. Whether connecting through[MCP](https://www.clueso.io/mcp) needs its own security approval came up on 10, all in 2026. Some of the late-2026 rise in the security line comes from these questions.


We'll cover agent access in its own post. The narrower point here is that once a video tool can log in to your product or read your code, IT reviews it like any other system with that access, and buyers have started raising those questions on early calls. If you're curious how teams actually use agents for video once they're approved, our[analysis of 45,000 videos](https://www.clueso.io/blog/ai-agent-video-study) found that agents built 19% of new Clueso videos in October 2026.


## Budget is still the top question, and it's really a question about sign-off


None of this means price stopped mattering. Pricing came up on 59.8% of all buyer calls, more than any other topic. But the most-asked question in the whole data set wasn't "how much?". It was "how do we get budget approved, and does the timing fit our budget cycle?", which came up on 113 calls.


The questions around it point the same way. "I need sign-off from my boss, finance, or IT. Who decides, and what can I take to them?" came up on 79 calls. How long procurement will take on the buyer's own side came up on 66. Help building the ROI case for leadership came up on 51. "What's the pricing unit: seats, export hours, credits, or videos?" came up on 71, from buyers who wanted to forecast the bill and avoid surprise overages.


Put together, the commercial conversation looks a lot like buying any shared system. The person on the call often couldn't approve the purchase, so they needed numbers someone above them would accept. If you're building that case now, our[template for a CFO-friendly business case](https://www.clueso.io/blog/business-case-for-video-creation-software) covers the numbers finance will ask for.


## The product questions that grew are about running a library, not making one video


The product questions shifted in the same direction. The ones that grew in 2026 ask whether a tool can keep producing at volume while someone stays in control of the output.


"We need dozens or hundreds of videos a month. Can a small team keep up?" came up on 55 calls, 34 of them in 2026. Keeping videos current when the UI changes came up on 58, and it grew about as fast as calls overall (31 of them were in 2026). A newer question is about oversight: "How accurate is the generated content, and how much human review will it need?" came up on 26 calls, and 24 of them were in 2026. Loading an existing brand kit came up on 21, with 19 of them in 2026.


A team asking these questions has already accepted that AI will make the videos, and it wants to know who checks the output and what happens to the library when the product ships again. We've written about why[maintaining product videos now costs more than making them](https://www.clueso.io/blog/product-video-maintenance-cost) , and it's the same concern showing up in the sales cycle.


## What this means if you're the one buying


If you lead customer education or product marketing, you're probably the one who found the tool and the one who has to get it approved. In a growing share of our calls, approval started before the evaluation did. Certification questions arrived on discovery calls, and AI councils stepped in before trials.


On those calls, the evaluation of the videos came second, and it couldn't start until the review was underway. In practice, the vendor's security documentation becomes part of what you're judging. If your IT team can read the vendor's answers on the day you find the tool, its review can start that day instead of after another round of calls. Our[guide to the questions enterprise buyers ask](https://www.clueso.io/blog/evaluating-enterprise-ai-video-tools) lists what each reviewing team asks for and what a good answer looks like.


At Clueso, the agentic video platform for businesses, we publish those answers where reviewers can check them without a call. Clueso is SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 certified, and our[pricing page](https://www.clueso.io/pricing) lists both on every plan, Free included. We don't use customer content to train AI models, and our[sub-processor list](https://www.clueso.io/legal/subprocessors) names the model providers behind each capability, with changes posted at least 10 business days before they take effect. Content is stored in the AWS region where a workspace is created: California, Frankfurt, or Mumbai. The AI providers that process it are US services, covered by Standard Contractual Clauses where they apply, and the sub-processor list says so. On the[Enterprise plan](https://www.clueso.io/enterprise) , an admin can restrict a workspace to an approved subset of AI and voice providers, so an AI council can approve the specific models that will see its content.


## How we analyzed 2,055 sales calls


**The calls.** We started from 3,150 recorded calls between May 17, 2024 and November 4, 2026. We dropped calls with no outside participant, no summary, under six minutes, or only agency and vendor contacts, which left 2,378. AI models then read the summary of each call and labelled 2,055 as buyer calls: discovery calls, demos, trials, security and procurement calls, onboarding, and renewals. The other 323 were partners, vendors, recruiting, investors, or internal.


**What we read in full.** We had AI models read the full transcripts of 80 calls end to end. We chose those calls because they carried the most security, procurement, pricing, and competitive discussion, and they produced 1,164 verbatim questions. For every other buyer call we worked from the call summary, which produced 4,028 paraphrased questions.


**How questions were grouped.** We merged all 5,192 questions into 267 distinct questions, and each one maps to exactly one. Every count in this post is the number of distinct calls where a question came up at least once. Topic shares count a call once per topic, and one call usually raises several topics. Half-year groupings follow the call date. "In 2026" means January 1 to November 4, 2026, which holds 1,083 of the 2,055 calls.


**The limits.**


- Summaries paraphrase and miss detail, so most questions are paraphrases. Only the 80 full transcripts are verbatim.
- The 80 transcripts were picked for commercial content, so they aren't a random sample.
- These are calls with one vendor. They reflect the companies that talk to us, which skews toward software companies and larger teams.
- A count shows that a question came up. It doesn't show whether it changed the outcome of a deal, and we didn't infer outcomes.
- How we grouped questions affects the counts. Pricing, for example, splits across many separately worded questions, which is why the certification question can top the discovery-call list while pricing tops the topic list.
- The first half-year has 152 calls and the last has 692, so the early percentages move more on a few calls.


We've kept company names, people, and quotes out of this post. Every number is an aggregate.


## Frequently asked questions


### Why are security reviews happening earlier in AI video purchases?


AI video tools take in company material, like product recordings, scripts, and internal processes, and send it to AI model providers to generate scripts, voiceovers, and visuals. That puts them under the same policies as any other AI system. In our calls, 78 of the 96 SOC 2 and ISO questions came on discovery or demo calls, and an AI council requirement came up on 26 calls, often before a trial could begin.


### What does an AI governance committee want to know about an AI video tool?


Committees ask whether the vendor trains models on your content, which AI providers process it, where it's stored, and whether the tool can be limited to providers you've approved. Some also ask about voice cloning and avatar consent. Our[guide to enterprise AI video evaluations](https://www.clueso.io/blog/evaluating-enterprise-ai-video-tools) covers what a good answer to each looks like.


### Does Clueso use customer videos to train AI models?


No. Clueso doesn't use your videos, recordings, transcripts, or other content to train AI models, and its AI sub-processors confirm in writing that they won't either. The[sub-processor list](https://www.clueso.io/legal/subprocessors) names each provider by capability, and the[data processing agreement](https://www.clueso.io/legal/dpa) sets a 10-business-day notice period for changes.


### Where does Clueso store customer data, and can we limit which AI providers it uses?


Clueso stores content on AWS in California, Frankfurt, or Mumbai, depending on where your workspace is created, so a Frankfurt workspace stores its content in the EU. The AI providers that process content are US services, and the sub-processor list covers those transfers. On the Enterprise plan, an admin can restrict a workspace to an approved subset of AI and voice providers. Our[FAQ](https://www.clueso.io/faqs) covers SSO, encryption, and the rest of the security basics.


Of the 26 calls where an AI council came up, 22 happened in 2026. If you're about to bring an AI video tool into your company, ask your IT or legal team this week whether an AI council exists, and what it needs to see before anyone can run a trial.
